title: What is an anonymous class, when do you use it, what are its restrictions (no constructor, no static members, single base type), and how does it compare to lambdas?
shortTitle: Anonymous classes — what they are, when to use them, their restrictions, and how they compare to lambdas

s1_definition.profdef: An anonymous class is a local class without a name that is declared and instantiated in a single expression. It extends exactly one class or implements exactly one interface, and its body provides the implementation inline at the point of use. It cannot declare an explicit constructor because it has no name to attach one to, it cannot declare static members other than constant static fields, and it captures effectively-final local variables from the enclosing scope.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India and needs a one-time signatory for a single cheque. Instead of hiring a permanent, named employee for that one task, the branch manager grabs any available person, hands them a form with the exact instructions written on it, and that person signs just this once and is never seen again. There is no need to give that temporary helper a name, a job title, or a desk — they exist only for this single transaction. That throwaway, nameless, one-task helper is an anonymous class.
s1_definition.oneliner: An anonymous class is a nameless, one-shot subclass or interface implementation written inline where it is used, with no constructor and no instance static members.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An anonymous class is a local class without a name that is declared and instantiated in a single expression. It extends exactly one class or implements exactly one interface, and its body provides the implementation inline at the point of use. It cannot declare an explicit constructor because it has no name to attach one to, it cannot declare static members other than constant static fields, and it captures effectively-final local variables from the enclosing scope.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India and needs a one-time signatory for a single cheque. Instead of hiring a permanent, named employee for that one task, the branch manager grabs any available person, hands them a form with the exact instructions written on it, and that person signs just this once and is never seen again. There is no need to give that temporary helper a name, a job title, or a desk — they exist only for this single transaction. That throwaway, nameless, one-task helper is an anonymous class.

**One line to remember:** An anonymous class is a nameless, one-shot subclass or interface implementation written inline where it is used, with no constructor and no instance static members.

sections.s2_technical:
An anonymous class is created with the `new` keyword followed by a class or interface name, a constructor-style argument list, and a body in braces. For example, to sort trades by amount you can pass a one-off comparator: `trades.sort(new Comparator<Trade>() { public int compare(Trade a, Trade b) { return a.getAmount().compareTo(b.getAmount()); } });`. Here `Comparator<Trade>` is the single base type, and the braces hold the inline implementation. The object is created immediately; the class has no name you can refer to anywhere else.

The first restriction is **no explicit constructor**. Because the class has no name, you cannot write a constructor for it — a constructor must share the class name, and there is none. You can still pass arguments in the `new` call, but those go to the superclass constructor. If you need initialisation logic, you use an instance initializer block instead: `new Account() {{ this.status = "ACTIVE"; }}`.

The second restriction is **a single base type**. An anonymous class can either extend one class or implement one interface, never both, and never more than one interface. For example `new Runnable() { public void run() { ... } }` implements exactly one interface. If you genuinely need to both extend a class and implement several interfaces, you must write a named class.

The third restriction is **no static members** except compile-time constant static final fields. You cannot declare static methods or mutable static fields inside an anonymous class, because an anonymous class is inherently an instance tied to its enclosing context, not a standalone named type that owns class-level state.

Anonymous classes **capture effectively-final local variables**. If the enclosing method has a local variable such as `BigDecimal fee`, the anonymous class may read it only if it is never reassigned after initialisation. This is because the captured value is copied into the anonymous instance, so allowing reassignment would create confusing, inconsistent copies.

Compared to **lambdas**, the key difference is that a lambda can only implement a functional interface — an interface with exactly one abstract method. An anonymous class can implement an interface with many methods or extend a concrete class. Inside a lambda, `this` refers to the enclosing instance, whereas inside an anonymous class `this` refers to the anonymous object itself. Lambdas do not introduce a new scope for `this` and do not generate a separate class file in the same way; the compiler uses `invokedynamic` and a generated method. A senior nuance is that lambdas are more memory-efficient and clearer for single-method callbacks, so modern Java prefers a lambda wherever the target is a functional interface, and reserves anonymous classes for multi-method interfaces, extending classes, or when you need instance state or `this` to mean the implementation object.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a nightly job that must process a list of pending transfers, and each transfer needs a one-off callback that reacts when the transfer finishes. We do not want to create a permanent named class for every tiny callback variation; we need a throwaway implementation written right where it is used. This is exactly what an anonymous class gives us — a nameless, inline implementation of a callback interface.

Problem 2 — The bank needs to sort today's trades by amount for a report, and this sort rule is used in only one place. Writing a whole named `Comparator` class file for a single use is wasteful. An anonymous `Comparator` captures the rule inline. We will also show the same rule written as a lambda to compare the two styles directly.

Problem 3 — Some callbacks need a multi-method listener interface, where a lambda cannot be used because the interface has more than one abstract method. This shows precisely when an anonymous class is still required and a lambda is not an option.

In the mini-project we build a `TransferService` that accepts a `TransferListener` (a multi-method interface) and a single-method `TransferCallback` (a functional interface). We register one listener as an anonymous class, one callback as an anonymous class, and the same callback again as a lambda, and we sort trades with both an anonymous comparator and a lambda, logging everything so the reader sees behaviour and the `this` difference.

The code contains: a `TransferCallback` functional interface, a `TransferListener` multi-method interface, a `Trade` and `Account` model, a `TransferService`, and a `main` exercising anonymous classes versus lambdas.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, balance 1,000,000) transfers rent of 50,000 to Priya (CUR3001, balance 250,000), once using an anonymous callback and once using a lambda callback. We also sort three trades.

Step 1 — The `main` method creates two `Account` objects and a `TransferService`. The accounts hold their balances in `BigDecimal` so no rounding errors ever occur with money.

Step 2 — We register a `TransferListener` as an anonymous class. Because `TransferListener` has two abstract methods, a lambda is impossible here; the anonymous class supplies both `onStart` and `onComplete` inline. The listener reference is stored inside the service.

Step 3 — We build two `TransferCallback` values: one as an anonymous class and one as a lambda. Both are valid because `TransferCallback` has a single abstract method. They are behaviourally identical for this single-method case.

Step 4 — The first `transfer` runs. The service fires `listener.onStart`, debits Rajesh from 1,000,000 to 950,000, credits Priya from 250,000 to 300,000, then invokes the anonymous callback with the reference and success flag, then fires `listener.onComplete`.

Step 5 — The second `transfer` runs the same way but invokes the lambda callback. Rajesh goes from 950,000 to 900,000 and Priya from 300,000 to 350,000.

Step 6 — We sort the trade list with an anonymous `Comparator` (ascending by amount), then re-sort with a lambda comparator (descending). Both produce correct, ordered output, showing the two syntaxes side by side.

    │ rajesh.debit   950,000 → 900,000

  trades.sort( new Comparator(){...} )   ascending  → [980, 2450, 15000]
  trades.sort( (a,b) -> ... )            descending → [15000, 2450, 980]

sections.s6_takeaway:
An anonymous class is a local class without a name that I declare and instantiate in one expression, extending exactly one class or implementing exactly one interface, with the implementation written inline at the point of use. Its defining restrictions are that it cannot declare an explicit constructor because it has no name to attach one to, it cannot declare static members other than compile-time constants, it can have only a single base type, and it may read only effectively-final local variables from the enclosing method. When I need initialisation I use an instance initializer block instead of a constructor.

In my banking project I use anonymous classes mainly for listeners that have more than one method. For example, my transfer service accepts a transfer listener with an onStart and an onComplete method, and because that interface has two abstract methods a lambda simply cannot implement it, so I pass an anonymous class that supplies both methods inline. For single-method callbacks, such as a result callback that just reports success, I prefer a lambda because it is shorter and clearer.

The comparison with lambdas is the part interviewers want to hear. A lambda can only target a functional interface, meaning an interface with exactly one abstract method, whereas an anonymous class can implement a multi-method interface or even extend a concrete class. The other crucial difference is the meaning of this: inside an anonymous class, this refers to the anonymous object itself, but inside a lambda, this refers to the enclosing instance, which matters when you capture or log state. Lambdas are also lighter at runtime because the compiler uses invokedynamic rather than always emitting a separate class file.

So my rule in practice is simple. If the target is a functional interface and I just need a small piece of behaviour, I write a lambda. If the interface has multiple methods, if I must extend a class, or if I need the implementation object's own identity through this, I write an anonymous class. This keeps the code concise where it can be and correct where it must be, which is exactly the judgment a bank's codebase needs.

---

keyPoints: Anonymous class: inline implementation with no name
Used for: one-time event handlers, callbacks, comparators
Can extend a class OR implement one interface (not both)
Captured variables must be effectively final
